sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A palindrome reads the same from left to right and right to left under a chosen comparison rule. A two-pointer check compares matching positions from the outside toward the centre.

Go strings contain bytes, while `[]rune(s)` exposes Unicode code points. With runes, move `left` forward and `right` backward until a pair differs or the pointers meet.

For example, `level` matches at `l/l` and `e/e`, then reaches its centre. The word `été` also works with runes even though its accented letters occupy more than one UTF-8 byte.

Case, spaces, punctuation, accents, and Unicode normalization are product rules. `A man, a plan...` is a palindrome only if the function deliberately ignores separators and case.

Use runes whenever non-ASCII text is valid input. Byte indexing is enough only when the contract explicitly limits input to single-byte characters such as ASCII.

sections.title: The core model: palindrome checking in Go
sections.content:
palindrome checking in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The invariant is simple: everything outside the two pointers has already matched. Each successful comparison shrinks the unchecked region by two. That gives linear time and, after converting to runes, linear space. An ASCII-only version can work directly on bytes with constant extra space.

sections.title: The practical decision: palindrome checking in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether palindrome checking in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

UTF-8 lets Go store text compactly, but a character may span several bytes. Rune conversion is the straightforward interview choice when code-point comparison is intended. Full user-facing text can be more complex because a displayed character may contain multiple code points; the function contract should not promise more normalization than it performs.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: palindrome checking in Go
sections.content:
Failures around palindrome checking in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

A byte loop can appear correct for English tests and fail only after production receives other scripts. The bug is hidden by the test data. Add at least one multi-byte case and inspect `len(s)` beside `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)` to show why byte positions are not character positions.

sections.title: The important trade-off: palindrome checking in Go
sections.content:
palindrome checking in Go and reversing the whole value first solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Both common methods compare symmetric content. Two pointers express that relationship directly and can exit early. Creating a reversed rune slice may be convenient when the reversed value is also needed, but for a Boolean check it performs extra writes and allocation without improving the asymptotic time.
